title: The Margaree River, Cape Breton, NS
region_name: Margaree Valley, Inverness County, Cape Breton
intro_md:
The Margaree is Nova Scotia's most storied Atlantic salmon river — two branches, the Northeast Margaree and the Southwest Margaree, meeting at Margaree Forks and running on to the Gulf of St. Lawrence at Margaree Harbour. The Southwest branch is fed by Lake Ainslie, Nova Scotia's largest natural freshwater lake; the Northeast branch runs down through the Margaree Valley from headwaters above Big Intervale. The whole system — both branches plus Lake Ainslie — was designated a Canadian Heritage River in 1998, and the Margaree Salmon Museum at North East Margaree (Lee Wulff caught his first Atlantic salmon here in 1933) is one of North America's larger collections of angling history.

**All water and fishing rights on the Margaree are public** — unlike many New Brunswick salmon rivers, there is no leased private water here, and non-residents don't need a guide to fish for salmon. What is private is most of the land bordering the river, which is farmland — so reaching many named pools depends on longstanding local custom rather than a formal access system. The Margaree Salmon Association, the river's steward since 1982, publishes an official pools map with dozens of named spots and asks anglers to follow its etiquette guidance rather than assuming a right of way.

**Regulations overview, and a genuine complication worth knowing about.** The Margaree is officially Salmon Fishing Area 18, and its season dates and bag limits are issued under DFO **Maritimes** Region — different from the Gulf Region rules used for the Miramichi guide elsewhere in this app. But DFO **Gulf** Region separately publishes its own Atlantic salmon guide covering the Margaree, and Gulf Region's own science branch does the river's stock assessments. In practice the numbers match across both, but don't assume this river follows the same regional office as the Miramichi's — it sits administratively astride both. A Nova Scotia angling licence plus a separate salmon licence are required; the river is fly-only and 100% catch-and-release for salmon, and non-residents genuinely don't need a guide, which is worth stating plainly since it surprises people used to New Brunswick's rules.

sections.heading: Atlantic Salmon
sections.body_md:
**Two runs**: a summer run from June through early September, well known locally for dry-fly fishing, and a fall run from mid-September through October bringing the bigger fish — averaging 8–12 lb with fish to 30–40 lb reported some years. The Margaree's fish run mostly as large salmon (two winters at sea) rather than a grilse-dominated return, and it holds the province's rod-and-reel record: a 52.5 lb salmon taken here in 1927.

**A genuine bright spot.** The Gulf-coast striped bass boom that's hurting salmon smolt survival on rivers like the Miramichi appears to have hit the Margaree less hard — multiple sources describe the Margaree's salmon population as having held up comparatively better through the same period, which is worth knowing if you're choosing between the two systems.

**Season, limits and gear (2026, SFA 18).** Most of the river and its tributaries: June 1–October 15. The main stem between the highway bridges (East Margaree bridge on the lower river, up to the Big Intervale bridges on the Northeast and the Scotsville bridge on the Southwest), excluding tributaries, runs a longer bright season to October 31. The Northeast Margaree above the Big Intervale bridges is a permanent spawning sanctuary, **closed to fishing year-round**. Every fish caught must be released — the daily retention limit is zero, and the daily release limit is 4 grilse and salmon combined. Only barbless artificial flies are permitted.

**Fees (2026).** Resident seasonal salmon licence $41.68, non-resident seasonal $156.08, non-resident 7-day $63.15, one-day (either) $29.79; anglers 16–17 and people with a disability fish free. A separate general fishing licence, not required for salmon, covers other species. As on New Brunswick rivers, the licence stub must be returned within seven days of the season's close, even to report you didn't fish.

**The Warm Water Protocol.** The Margaree is one of the Gulf-region-style rivers with a formal in-season closure mechanism, co-developed by DFO with the province, the Margaree Salmon Association, the Nova Scotia Salmon Association and the Atlantic Salmon Federation. It closes the lower river when the daily minimum water temperature hits 20°C for two consecutive days, and closes the upper Northeast Margaree too at 23°C for two consecutive days — reopening only once temperatures drop back and stay down, with supporting evidence like stable water levels and a cooling forecast. It's a real, active tool: the river closed under the protocol from July 17 to September 25 in 2025, after a stressful season of high temperatures and drought. Treat any closure notice as current-year and check before a summer trip rather than assuming last year's dates repeat.

sections.heading: Brook Trout and Brown Trout
sections.body_md:
**Sea-run brook trout** arrive in the estuary and lower river in early spring, often described locally as showing up alongside the season's first salmon — the Margaree Salmon Association's own announcement of the trout season opening is typically posted around the third week of April. Resident brook trout and brown trout are present throughout the system and its tributaries.

**Regulation**: province-wide, fishing for brook trout, brown trout, lake trout or rainbow trout is restricted to unbaited lures or artificial flies only for the whole month of September. The Margaree carries its own spring closure on top of that: the river is closed to fishing for all species from April 1–15 on the main stem downstream from the Big Intervale bridges (Northeast branch) and the Scotsville bridge (Southwest branch), not including tributaries — so the practical trout opener lands around April 16, close to but not always exactly matching the Association's own announced date.

spots.name: Margaree Forks
spots.description: Where the Northeast and Southwest branches meet, and home to the well-known Forks Pool — park behind the library and wade across at the top per local knowledge.

spots.name: Margaree Salmon Museum, North East Margaree
spots.description: 60 East Big Intervale Road. One of North America's largest collections of angling history, open seasonally (roughly late June to mid-October, Wednesday–Sunday); Lee Wulff's first Atlantic salmon came from this river in 1933.

spots.name: Big Intervale
spots.description: Northeast Margaree, near the boundary of the permanent spawning sanctuary upstream — several named pools (Wards Rock, Skye Lodge and others) sit just below it.

spots.name: Lake Ainslie
spots.description: Nova Scotia's largest natural freshwater lake, and the source of the Southwest Margaree — launches near Ainslie Village and MacKinnons campgrounds.

spots.name: Margaree Harbour
spots.description: Where the combined river meets the Gulf of St. Lawrence — the estuary and the start of the tidal water.
